                Key Takeaways
                                            Spotify and Claude are both down Tuesday morning.
                                            Downdetector shows tens of thousands of user reports for each platform.
                                            Spotfiy confirmed the outage in a post on X, while Anthropic confirm issues on its Claude status page.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're having trouble getting your Spotify playlists up and running this morning, you're not alone. The music streaming platform is currently down for tens of thousands of users, at least. Downdetector is showing roughly 40,000 reports since 9:31 a.m. ET, with the last batch of reports coming in at 10:24 a.m. Spotify confirmed the issue in a post on X, writing: "We're aware of some issues right now and are checking them out!" Curiously, Spotify's outage comes at the same time as an outage with Claude, the AI platform from Anthropic. Downdetector shows tens of thousands of user reports here as well, and Anthropic confirmed an ongoing issue with Claude: "We are investigating reports of degraded performance affecting claude.ai, platform.claude.com, the Claude API, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. We will provide an update as soon as possible."
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear why these services are down this morning, or if they are related. But in all likelihood, Spotify and Anthropic will get their platforms back up and running soon. Typically, these occasional outages are resolved in hours, if not minutes, barring a widespread problem, like an outage with a cloud hosting provider. Last year's AWS outage "broke the internet," as did November's Cloudflare outage. There's no reason to think that's the case with these outages at this time.

title: You Could Lose Your Access to 'Old Reddit' Forever, but There's a Workaround
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio

        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Tim Goode/PA Images via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Reddit is making changes to how users can access Old Reddit, the legacy version of the site.
                                            Soon, users will need to use Old Reddit once every six months, otherwise they'll lose access.
                                            Reddit previously made Old Reddit accessible only to logged-in users back in July.
                                            One workaround is to become a mod, since moderators won't have to adhere to this new change.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        "Old Reddit" is the only way I use Reddit. That's not the case for most of the tech in my life. I don't make a point of only using an iPhone from a decade ago, or avoid playing video games with more than 64 bits. But, in my view, Old Reddit is the only proper way to use the website. While "new" Reddit has more "features," it's bloated and slow. Old Reddit might be extremely basic, and looks about the same as it did when I first started "redditing," but it works. Unfortunately, most of us likely won't be able to experience Old Reddit for much longer. On Wednesday, Reddit announced a series of infrastructure changes on its r/modnews subreddit. Normally, these updates wouldn't make tech headlines—I can't say Reddit "mod news" often finds its way into my feeds. But as part of these changes, Reddit confirmed a rather massive deprecation: Users will lose access to Old Reddit unless they've used the platform sometime in the last six months. It's not enough to use Reddit itself, mind you: Unless you use Old Reddit at least once in a six-month period, you'll lose access for good. This builds on a previous Old Reddit change the company rolled out over the summer, which requires users to be logged in in order to access this version of Reddit. While we don't have a true deadline for when these new changes take effect, the new announcement makes it clear that, "in the next few months, we’ll further limit access for logged-in users to only those who have used Old Reddit in the last six months (which covers the vast majority of all Old Reddit users).” The only exception is for moderators.
Why is Reddit going after Old Reddit?According to Reddit, these changes are designed to prevent abuse on its platform. By forcing users to log in to use Old Reddit, the company says it prevents unauthenticated access, its "largest source of abusive scraping and automated traffic." By blocking accounts that haven't accessed Old Reddit in the past six months, Reddit says it's solving another problem: Now, bad actors won't be able to make Reddit accounts for the sole purpose of accessing (and scraping) Old Reddit and its content. In Reddit's view, these changes don't affect Old Reddit users. If you rely on Old Reddit, the company thinks you'll be using it frequently enough to bypass these new rules. As such, Reddit believes the vast majority of affected users will only be those trying to abuse Old Reddit, not those who actively use it. The problem is, not everyone who uses Old Reddit is so steadfast. These new rules mean you can no longer take an extended break from Old Reddit and expect to return in the future. Sure, Reddit will always be there, but you'll lose access to the "best" version of the platform, as so many believe it to be. As this is the second change to Old Reddit in a short period of time, it begs the question: Is Reddit trying to shut down Old Reddit? That's what Ars Technica asked the company, and received the following in response:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
"As [Reddit CEO Steve Huffman previously] confirmed, Reddit is continuing to work on the future of Old Reddit. This change is about limiting unauthenticated access and reducing automated abuse—not removing Old Reddit for people and moderators who rely on it. We want to preserve Old Reddit for the real people that use it, not let it be a vector for automated abuse."How to continue using Old Reddit  Per the rules, the easiest way to continue using Old Reddit is to simply keep using it. If you've never done so before, you can head to old.reddit.com and sign into your account when prompted. As long as you access this version of the site at least once every six months, you'll maintain your access—assuming Reddit doesn't change the rules again.But if you want a more permanent fix without having to worry about visiting Old Reddit twice a year, become a mod. Moderators don't have the same requirements; simply being a mod gives them perpetual access to the site. The easiest way to become a mod is to simply start your own subreddit. If you have access to Old Reddit, you'll see this on the front page as "Create your own subreddit." If you're on new Reddit, you'll see this as "Start a community" under the three-lined menu. Reddit will walk you through the rest, asking you to answer questions or fill out responses about your new community. Assuming the subreddit isn't already taken, you'll be able to create it at the end, at which point you will automatically become a mod of your new subreddit.

title: Why a Test Can't Tell You Your 'Biological Age'
body:
Meredith Dietz
                            
        
            Meredith Dietz
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceMeredith is a marathon runner and stand-up comedian. As Lifehacker’s Senior Staff Writer, she covers personal fitness tech, home gym equipment, and more.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

    Table of Contents
    
        
        It's not enough to live forever—everybody wants to stay young forever, too. In most wellness spaces, "youth" is a word that gets thrown around as synonymous with "health," but you don't have to be into woo-woo wellness culture to find yourself tempted to find out how old—or more accurately, how young—you really are. Maybe you can't fight your chronological age, but you can find comfort in an alternative framing: "biological age."The pitch is appealing. Send in a vial of blood or a tube of spit, pay several hundred dollars, and receive a number that supposedly reveals your "true" biological age. The promise is that this age is the one your body is actually living, as opposed to the one on your driver's license. If you find out you're "biologically" 35 instead of 45, the implication is that you've pulled one over on the passage of time. Discover the reverse, and the tests often come bundled with supplements, programs, or subscriptions designed to fix your problems.The real problem is that biological age isn't actually a single figure that can be measured or calculated, and no test—however promising the science behind it—can hand you a definitive verdict on how your body is aging. Here's what's actually going on inside these tests, what legitimate research says about aging, and how to think about the growing market of products promising to quantify your youth.
What does "biological age" even mean?Chronological age is easy: you count the years since you were born. Biological age is an attempt to pin down how well your body is actually functioning relative to that timeline. Dr. Dan Belsky, an epidemiologist at Columbia University who studies aging, explains it this way: Everyone moves through calendar time at the same rate, but "the conditions inside our body obviously vary." Because health tends to decline over time, biological age is essentially an estimate of the age at which a person's physiological integrity—how well their organs and tissues function, resist stress, and recover from injury—would be considered typical within some reference group.That last part is key. "There really is no ground truth biological age, because it's always relative to some expectation," Belsky says. Saying you're "biologically 25" only means something once you know what factors you're being judged on, and what standards you're being compared to. A biological age score is a construct built from a specific reference population, which could be a large, nationally representative sample, or a much smaller research cohort. That detail is key to understanding how much weight any individual result should carry.There is no one biomarker that determines your "true" ageConsumer biological age tests love to reduce aging to a single number, but researchers who study aging combine many types of data to get anywhere close to a meaningful picture. That typically includes laboratory-based biomarkers, like the kind of bloodwork your doctor might order during an annual physical. Those biomarkers are then placed alongside clinical measurements like blood pressure, heart rate, and imaging. Increasingly, researchers also look at molecular and cellular markers, including genes and proteins.One of the most talked-about approaches in recent years uses "epigenetic clocks," which look at chemical modifications to your DNA (rather than the DNA sequence itself) and compare the pattern to population averages to estimate biological age. Several companies now sell consumer versions of this technology, generally priced around $300, using blood or saliva samples.According to Belsky, at their best, these commercial tests are "a consumer implementation of a research tool." In practice, that means a lab takes an algorithm developed using a specific research dataset and applies it to your individual sample. The algorithm was built to describe patterns across groups, not to diagnose an individual person, which is part of why a single test result can deliver an unreliable personal verdict. What can (and cannot) impact someone's biological ageWhen it comes to what actually shapes biological aging, the answer is "almost everything," Belsky says. Genetics play a role in how resilient a person's body is over time. But environmental and behavioral factors are often just as important, if not more so. The quality of the water you drink and the air you breathe, your diet, and the stability and meaningfulness of your social relationships are critical. Sleep, exercise, and nutrition tend to dominate the public conversation, and for good reason, but they're part of a much longer list of contributing factors.This is also where biological age intersects with inequality. Research has consistently linked poverty, pollution, and unstable living conditions to accelerated biological aging and shorter lifespans. Not everyone has equal access to fresh food, clean air, safe housing, or reliable medical care—and those disparities show up in the body over time. A biological age test can't account for the structural conditions someone is navigating; it can only reflect the downstream biological signal.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Can you reverse or slow your biological age?This is where the marketing gets ahead of the science. Many products claim you can measurably "reverse" your biological age through supplements, specific diets, or intensive protocols. The research, naturally, is more cautious. From the standpoint of how most people intuitively understand biological age (as a general reflection of your body's current state), yes, that state can be modified through better health habits. But whether behavioral, environmental, or pharmacological interventions actually change the pace of aging at the cellular level in humans? There we have "less clarity," Belsky says.Of course, living a healthier life will generally support how your body functions, and likely influence the biomarkers that feed into these tests. But claims that a particular product has been shown to "reverse" cellular aging in a rigorous, replicated way should always be treated with skepticism. Despite the promises of certain longevity influencers, there's no evidence that any supplement, cold plunge protocol, or red light therapy device will add decades to your life. It's also worth reframing the goal. Healthy aging isn't really about looking younger than your birth certificate suggests, or avoiding every illness. Instead, it could be more productive to think in terms of a broader health span: the stretch of life you spend active, capable, and free of major disability. That means building habits that help your body adapt as it inevitably changes with time, rather than wasting your time, money, privacy, and mental health in the pursuit of a lower number on a test result.What to know before buying a biological age testIf you are itching to find out your "true" age, consider treating your score as a simple data point, as opposed to a catch-all verdict.  "People often want a yardstick to track progress toward personal wellness goals," Belsky says, "and the best-evidenced tests have at least been studied in research settings, so there's some understanding of how their scores relate to disease risk, disability, mortality, and in some cases, how responsive they are to interventions." At the same time, "these are not standalone, one-shot measurements you can trust to reveal the full truth about your health." Like any biomedical test, they're subject to bias and error, and they need to be interpreted alongside other health information, ideally with a healthcare professional.Before spending a few hundred dollars on a biological age test, it's worth asking yourself a more practical question: Let's say you find out your body is aging "faster" than your birthday suggests—how would you actually change your behavior? Perhaps a biological age test is the helpful nudge you need to jump-start habits you've been meaning to build anyway. But if you already generally know the factors that support long-term health—moving your body, eating well, sleeping enough, managing stress, maintaining relationships, avoiding smoking, and so on and so forth—maybe you can start making those changes today, no vial of blood required.

        Spotlight is the gateway to everything on my iPhone. From looking up contacts to toggling obscure features, I use Spotlight every day to get things done. But while many of us use it, I don't think most use Spotlight to its fullest potential. Yes, it's a way to search for things on your iPhone, but it's also a "launcher" for automations, a calculator, a currency converter, and a way to run tasks inside your favorite apps. If you have an iPhone, these are 10 Spotlight search hacks you should know.
Bypass the Clock app to set timers, alarms, or to use the stopwatchThe Clock app lets you set timers, alarms, and set a stopwatch, too. Normally, you'd launch the Clock app to access all those features on your iPhone, but Spotlight lets you bypass that. Open Spotlight on your iPhone, and search for "Clock." The top results will be: Clock, Set Timer, Add Alarm, and Stopwatch. Tap any of the last three buttons to run those features from your iPhone's Dynamic Island.Tapping "Set Timer" shows a slider to choose the timer's length. Similarly, "Add Alarm" lets you set an alarm without opening Clock, and "Stopwatch" immediately starts the count, and even lets you pause or set a lap time without opening the app.
Locate text in photos and screenshots via Spotlight searchYour iPhone has built-in OCR (optical character recognition), which means that it can identify, select, and copy text in photos and screenshots. Spotlight lets you search for text in images without opening the Photos app. Just fire up Spotlight and search for a word or a phrase. The "Photos" section of results will show you all images containing your search term.Convert units and currencies without opening websites or apps
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
I grew up in a country that follows the metric system, and I just can't wrap my head around Imperial units used in the U.S. and U.K. Every time I read something that mentions gallons, fluid ounces, miles, stones, or other units that should've been retired in the 19th century, I use Spotlight to convert them quickly. Try searching for "1 inch to cm," or similar terms with different units, and the result will display at the top. For currency conversions, type the currency symbol followed by the amount, and Spotlight will convert it to your local currency by default. Try searching for "£120" or "$240," and the converted currency will show up in the results. You can also try a more specific query such as "£360 to USD" to convert to a currency of your choice.Perform calculations in Spotlight's search boxI rarely open the calculator on my iPhone. When I need to perform basic math, I fire up Spotlight and type the calculation. It works with addition, subtraction, division, multiplication, and even percentages. The syntax for calculations is straightforward in Spotlight, but to get percentages, you'll want to try something like "20% x 180." This is great for calculating tips or splitting bills.Type any date to create a calendar entry or to find photosYou can use Spotlight to quickly add calendar entries. Activate Spotlight on your iPhone, type a future date, and tap the Add button in the Event widget. This will open a Calendar entry page, and allow you to add the event without opening the Calendar app. You can also search for specific months from the past, such as "October 2024" to look for photos, messages, and emails from that month. The results show up in neatly organized sections under each app's name, and tapping a result takes you to specific photos, messages, or emails.Type "Record" to start a voice recording
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
Spotlight also allows you to start a voice recording quickly. Type "Record" to reveal results related to the Voice Memos app on your iPhone. Tap the Record button to record a voice note, and it'll show a timer and a stop recording button in your iPhone's Dynamic Island.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Download videos from Instagram, Threads, or YouTube directly from SpotlightIf you use iPhone automations to download videos from Instagram, Threads, or YouTube, you can run these directly from Spotlight. Just search "Download" in Spotlight, and the shortcuts named "Download Instagram," "Download Threads," and "YouTube Download" will appear in the results. As long as you have a video URL from one of those sites copied to the clipboard, tapping the respective shortcuts will instantly begin downloading the video. This is perfect for times when you receive a social media link in a messaging app. You can copy it, then run the automation via Spotlight.Use Spotlight to enable greyscale mode when you want to eliminate distractionsI use this automation every day to reduce my smartphone usage. Searching for "Color Filters" lets me toggle that setting directly from Spotlight, and enables greyscale mode when I need to focus on work. Disabling this feature is just as easy. If you use any other feature that is buried deep in iOS settings, you can use Spotlight to search for it, and toggle it as needed.Type "Focus" to toggle various DND modes on your iPhoneThe search bar is not the most obvious place for switching between different Focus modes on your iPhone, but it works quite well. Just type "Focus" in Spotlight search, and it'll list multiple DND modes, allowing you to toggle the one you need. These results appear in the "Settings" section in Spotlight's search results.Check iOS Settings to hide apps and content from SpotlightYou can also hide apps and search results from Spotlight. This is a good way to keep dating apps or sensitive data away from results. To set this up, go to Settings > Search on your iPhone. Under "Before Searching," tap the drop-down menu next to "Suggest Apps." Choose "Don't suggest" if you want to hide all app suggestions from Spotlight. Instead, you can use your iPhone's App Library to find and launch apps faster.If that feels a bit extreme, scroll down to find individual apps you want to hide from Spotlight. Tap the app's name, and disable "Show App in Search." To hide results from that app in Spotlight, disable "Show Content in Search" on the same page. You'll have to do this once per app.

But while all these new products are objective upgrades over their predecessors, they all have one issue in common: They keep randomly rebooting. 
What is Apple's rebooting problem?As reported by 9to5Mac, some iPhone 18 Pro users are noticing that their smartphones are freezing up after a failed Face ID scan. When this happens, you won't be able to interact with your iPhone, even if the "Try Face ID Again" button appears onscreen. Instead, after a few moments, the iPhone will reboot. Some analyses showed that the Neural Engine was at fault, but Apple never confirmed the exact issue.

Apple released watchOS 27.0.1 exclusively for Series 12 and Ultra 4 users on Wednesday, Sept. 23, which it says should fix random reboots going forward. body:
When you think of local AI, you might assume that running models on local hardware instead of paying for cloud-based services is the safer and more private option. That’s only partially true. When running AI locally, you maintain better control over your workflows and data. You decide whether to share your data with any third-party services, and if so, under what terms. You also don’t have to worry about data breaches and cyberattacks targeting major tech corporations. But on the other hand, you refuse the multimillion-dollar security infrastructure built by established players like OpenAI or Anthropic. Your security is now fully your responsibility, for better or worse. With that in mind, here are ten clever hacks to help you achieve better security when running AI models on your PC or a private VPS (virtual private server). Is it safer to run AI models on local hardware?When running AI models on your personal hardware using a platform like Jan, Ollama, or LM Studio, your messages, documents, and chat history do not leave your device and aren’t sent to someone else’s cloud servers. If you’re worried about an AI company selling your data without your consent, or if you don’t want to end up with your credentials leaked in the next data breach, going local is the smart move. That said, it isn’t foolproof. You’re still downloading the AI model files from a public database. You may also have to let the model access certain APIs so it can talk to your software or data over the public web. Finally, if you’re using a public wifi, anyone else connected to the network may be able to breach your operating system by targeting the AI. In other words, things are not as simple as people sometimes make them out to be. 
Just this January, SentinelOne and Censys found 175,000 publicly exposed Ollama hosts that could be used by any attacker with an internet connection to execute code and connect to third-party services from a user’s credentials and hardware. If you want to run AI locally, you have to be very careful with where you get your models from and what they have access to. Here are some tips to help you get it right.Keep your model server on localhostTo run AI models on your local machine, you’ll need to use an inference engine (also called a runner) like Ollama or LM Studio, which let the model load and execute on your hardware. By default, AI runners are configured to run models on localhost (127.0.0.1 or 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1), meaning that other devices on your network or the public web can’t access it. But if you run your AI model on 0.0.0.0, that opens up access to all devices in your network. Anyone on your shared wifi can boot up your local AI setup, then use it to make changes to your hardware or steal sensitive data.Sometimes, setup guides will suggest that you do this anyway, so that you can access your local AI model from other devices on your network, like a smartphone or laptop. It also comes up when people try to run AI models on VPS servers or Network-Attached Storage (NAS) devices. But this will put your data and workflows at risk, so if you did something to change the default server configuration of your model runner, make sure to change it back now: On Ollama, you can do this by changing the OLLAMA_HOST variable back to 127.0.0.1. For LM Studio, toggle off “Serve on Local Network."If you use Jan, click the gear icon on your Hub interface to get to the Settings page. Then select Local API Server and make up an API key using an online generator like RandomKeygen.Use a private VPN tunnel instead of port forwardingYou shouldn’t expose your AI model to your public IP address on the internet. But what if you still need to share model access to your other devices remotely? Normally, people enable port forwarding on their routers to configure access to their resources and data from a remote location. But you should never use this approach to configure remote access to AI models or runners on your local machine. If you’re already running your AI model on 0.0.0.0, and you choose to enable port forwarding on your router on top of that, anyone on the internet can break into your local AI setup if they manage to guess your IP address. Cyber attackers often operate bot networks that routinely scan the internet for open ports on residential IPs, so you're running the risk of being targeted if you do this. A better way is to set up an encrypted tunnel using a VPN or Cloudflare ZTNA. Mesh VPNs like Tailscale are a popular choice for this, as is Cloudflare Zero Trust’s new Tunnel feature. Update your AI runner as soon as patches landIn May 2026, Cyera uncovered a new Ollama vulnerability that let attackers steal chunks of your data and credentials using unauthenticated API calls. The flaw, called “Bleeding Llama,” had a CVSS rating of 9.3 out of 10. At the time, it put around 300,000 publicly exposed Ollama servers at risk until it was addressed in patch version 0.17.1. AI runners like LM Studio, Ollama, Jan, and GPT4All are still experimental and often reveal new vulnerabilities that get patched in subsequent releases. If your runner is even a few versions out of date, your server could be vulnerable to a serious attack vector that hackers can exploit. Always grab the latest release as soon as you can from the AI runner’s official website or GitHub repository.Choose safetensors or GGUF files over pickleAI models based on older deep learning models like PyTorch are often downloadable as pickle files, with extensions like .bin, .pt, or .pkl. But due to the nature of the Python pickle file format, these model files can be altered to execute malicious code as soon as you try to load them using your runner. Back in 2025, ReversingLabs found two live model files on Hugging Face that had cleared the platform’s automated security checks even though they had an unauthorized remote access function hidden in plain sight. Now, Hugging Face’s own documentation notes pickle files as a major security risk.  To avoid data breaches or unauthorized access, you should only download LLMs that come packaged in newer file formats like .safetensor or .gguf. These file formats store your data in numerical format, which makes malicious code execution impossible as a model loads. If a particular model is only available as a .pt  or .pkl file, I’d just skip it. There are plenty of newer-version LLMs that use more secure file formats. Download models from publishers you can verifyAI hubs like Hugging Face or ModelScope allow anyone with an internet connection to upload AI models to their website. While they have some platform-level security protocols in place, in cases like the incident discovered by ReversingLabs in 2025, newer or more sophisticated exploits can bypass these protocols and verifications very easily. For better safety, download model files uploaded from official accounts managed by major model developers only. For example, Google, Mistral, Meta, and Qwen (Alibaba) all have separate organizational accounts with a verified badge on Hugging Face.  Verification badges indicate that a company account is really owned and administered by that company, because the uploader would have had to use an official company email address to log in and upload the model files. You can see the Advanced Security section of Hugging Face’s documentation for more details on how verified badges work for enterprises.Get your AI apps from official websites onlyHackers like to use popular GenAI tools as a lure to get people to install malicious software. Often, they’ll set up fake websites or upload to popular app marketplaces where they can pose as official platforms. Earlier attempts focused on ChatGPT clones on lookalike websites that seemed like the real OpenAI. They would get people to download a corrupt .exe or .dmg file, which would then deliver dangerous payloads like Redline, Lumma, or the Odyssey infostealer for Mac. Similar attempts have also been used to target Android users through malicious apps uploaded to the Play Store. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
But the attacks have grown more sophisticated since then and may even target obscure local AI platforms and Python packages. Attackers have gone as far as to breach official GitHub repositories and Python Package Index (PyPI) uploads. TrendAI reported one particularly disturbing instance where malicious code was inserted directly into the official PyPI package of LiteLLM, an open-source AI gateway that lets you call hundreds of LLMs from a single API. Positive Security also discovered malicious Python packages uploaded to PyPI as Deepseek lookalikes. Make sure to verify where you’re getting your AI tools from. Your best bet is to rely on direct official sources, verified GitHub repos maintained by trusted AI vendors, and Python packages referenced directly in the source company’s official documentation.Double-check packages your model tells you to installI already covered how Python packages are corrupted to install malware as soon as you run them on your system. But it’s not just the LLM files and AI tools that you need to watch out for. When you ask AI agents to write code or execute tasks, they also install and run any packages or dependencies needed to complete that job. And because AI models are prone to hallucination, agents will often just make up package names that don’t exist. A recent study that analyzed 16 models across 576,000 code samples found that open-weight LLMs do this 21.7% of the time, while frontier AI models have a lower hallucination rate of 5.2%. Hackers know this, hence "slopsquatting," a new attack in which bad actors register fake software packages under commonly hallucinated package names across different LLMs. These packages can run malicious code, prompt injection attacks, or infostealers as soon as your AI agent runs them on your local machine. The best way to avoid these attacks is to limit what your AI agent can install and run without your approval. You can either choose to manually approve each software package before the model installs or runs it, or you can whitelist certain trustworthy repositories that aren’t likely to contain malware. Either way, make sure to review your model’s log to see what pip install and npm install commands it runs to avoid unauthorized installations.Limit what your AI agents can touchEven when you run them on your local hardware, AI agents can call MCP servers, download and run files, search the web, or connect to third-party services using APIs. Moreover, they can read and write files to your local hardware and even change core operating system settings. All of these features should be enabled only with an abundance of caution based on your security profile. Carefully manage the level of access an AI agent or model runner has on your system, especially newer open-weight models that are more likely to hallucinate or have exploitable vulnerabilities. There are multiple ways to regulate how much access an AI agent has. The first is to run your AI workflows inside a Dockerized container that can’t make direct changes to your system files. Beyond that, you can also restrict permissions by changing the default configuration of your agentic framework, like OpenClaw or Hermes. OpenClaw lets you choose between three default permission profiles, including ask, deny, and allowlist, which can be further scoped to specific workflows and services. Hermes also lets you set up a similar allowlist (whitelist) or restrict tool usage per cron job. Switch on local-only modeAI model runners like Ollama and LM Studio can support local as well as cloud-hosted models. But you can configure them to restrict network access through a single function even if you haven’t done so at the orchestration layer with Hermes or OpenClaw. You do this by binding the service to your local IP address (127.0.0.1) to prevent other devices from accessing it over your network or the public web.Encrypt the drive that holds your chat historyWhen you keep your AI workflows local, your entire chat history, along with any credentials, secrets, or API tokens you may have shared with your model, exist in plain text on your local drives. If someone managed to access your device physically, they could take all of it. Apps like FileVault, BitKocker, or LUKS can encrypt your hard drive so that your chat history can’t be read in plain text without an encryption key to decode it. Use them to avoid the risk of exposure if your device is stolen or lost.A few local AI platforms to get started withIf you’re new to local AI, here are a few platforms to play around with. They offer the best accessibility for new users who aren’t familiar with the technicalities of AI engineering. Ollama: An open-source model runner for macOS, Windows, and Linux. Large model library and a simple desktop app that most other local AI tools can plug into.LM Studio: A polished desktop app that lets you download models from Hugging Face inside a graphical UI. It's been free for both work and personal use since July 2025.Jan: An open-source, Apache 2.0-licensed ChatGPT alternative that runs fully offline on Windows, macOS, and Linux.AnythingLLM Desktop: A free MIT-licensed app for chatting with your own documents locally. It's a solid pick if you want to feed PDFs and notes to a model without uploading them anywhere.Open WebUI: A browser-based offline chat interface that can connect to Ollama and make the UI more accessible. Pair it with a mesh VPN, and your whole household can use one AI server safely.

title: Apple Intelligence Is Taking Up Way More Storage Than Apple Promised on These Devices
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple Intelligence, Apple's suite of AI features, is taking up more space than it's supposed to.
                                            On some Macs, Apple Intelligence is taking upwards of 30GB of storage, when Apple says it should take up to 14GB.
                                            It isn't clear how to turn off Apple Intelligence, or clear this storage.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple's latest updates are all about AI—Apple Intelligence, that is. When you update to iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple will invite you to try Siri AI and other new Apple Intelligence features. (Assuming your iPhone supports Apple's AI features.) But whether you use the new AI-powered Siri all the time or find yourself frequently scrolling past the AI additions, Apple Intelligence is taking up space on your device—perhaps requiring more storage than you bargained for.I'll admit, I didn't think much of it when I updated my iPhone and Mac to the latest versions. I gave Siri AI a shot, adjusted Liquid Glass, and went back to doing pretty much the same things I was doing before I made the update. But once I saw headlines about how much storage Apple Intelligence actually takes up on these new updates, I had to see for myself. And, wow, were the headlines right: On my iPhone 17 Pro, Apple Intelligence alone takes up 20.65GB. On my M3 MacBook Pro, it takes up a solid 30GB. These numbers will vary by device: My M1 iMac, for example, only has 13.88GB allocated to Apple Intelligence. But still, these are large slices of my overall storage. Anyone with a small SSD knows how valuable each gigabyte really is, and upwards of 30GB for Apple Intelligence is a lot. Not only that, it's often more space than Apple's own metrics suggest: As MacRumors highlights, Apple says that Apple Intelligence should only take up to 14GB of storage at most, and even less for certain devices. So why is my MacBook Pro allocating more than double that space for Apple's AI? 
Why does Apple Intelligence take up so much storage on iPhone and Mac?I can't answer why Apple Intelligence is taking up so much more storage space than Apple says it should. But I can explain why Apple says its AI is supposed to occupy as much as 14GB on certain devices: Apple Intelligence is designed to run on-device whenever possible. While Apple does push certain tasks to its Private Cloud Compute platform, the company wants its AI models to run on your iPhone or Mac whenever possible. This safeguards your privacy, as none of your data has to leave your device to achieve the task—though Apple says Private Cloud Compute also protects your privacy throughout the entire process.   Regardless, for this reason, your iPhone or Mac will download Apple Intelligence models directly onto your device, so it can run processes on-device when it makes sense to do so. If you have a newer or more powerful device that supports Apple's more demanding AI features, like personalized Siri voices, you may need to store more Apple Intelligence data on-device to run those processes—up to 14GB for certain devices—yet it's not clear why Apple Intelligence takes up more than double that storage limit on some devices, like my MacBook Pro.     
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Check how much storage Apple Intelligence takes up on your devicesIt's easy to check how much storage Apple Intelligence is taking up on your device, though Apple doesn't make it obvious. To start, head to System Settings > General > Storage (macOS) or Settings > General > iPhone Storage (iOS). Scroll down and choose either "macOS (i)" or "iOS," respectively. Here, you'll see your system storage breakdown, including a figure for "Apple Intelligence."There's no solution at this pointUnfortunately, there doesn't appear to be a way to tell iOS or macOS to remove some Apple Intelligence models while leaving others intact, or to run all processes through Private Cloud Compute. In fact, it doesn't seem like there is any reliable way to disable Apple Intelligence on a device running iOS 27 or macOS 27 at all. The closest option I can find is to disable Siri (Settings or System Settings > Siri > Turn Off Siri), but while this disables a host of Apple Intelligence options, I still see the models taking up storage on my device, even after a restart. This might be one for Apple to fix in a future software update—hopefully as part of iOS 27.2.

title: I Tried Snap Specs, and They Could Be the Future of Smart Glasses
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”

    Table of Contents
    
        
        Snap was in the smart glasses game from the jump. The company’s original camera-equipped Spectacles debuted back in 2016, beating Meta to the market by five years. Meta’s Ray-Bans and Oakleys captured massive consumer mindshare anyway, while Snap’s smart eyewear has been less visible. With Snap Specs, though, the company is aiming to make up for lost time by delivering smart glasses that go beyond a hidden camera and voice-activated AI. At the Snapdragon 2026 Summit, I got my hands (and eyes) on a pair of Snap’s soon-to-be-released spatial-computing glasses that overlay digital graphics onto the physical world.Specs are heavy on tech but light on your face
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
There's a lot of tech packed into these black polymer frames. They're powered by two Snapdragon processors, with two full-color hi-res cameras facing outward; the tracking system supports 6DOF (six degrees of freedom) hand tracking for gesture controls; and it's all standalone, as there's no tether or wired puck handling the heavy lifting. With all that crammed into the frames, plus the battery to run it, you'd expect them to be heavy. At around 135 grams, they aren’t light, but Specs are surprisingly comfortable. The weight is distributed evenly, mainly across the frames, so for the brief time I used them, they remained ergonomically acceptable. Specs feel more like a pair of sunglasses than a bulky VR helmet. As for battery life, Snap promises four hours of mixed-use on a full charge. 
Display quality on Snap SpecsIn the interest of not alienating the people around you, Snap chose to make the lenses clear enough that your eyes can still be seen through them, but if you want to close out the world, there’s electrochromic dimming for quick transitions between clear and dark lenses. It both useful and a cool trick. Check it out:
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
The in-glasses display is surprisingly bright. Specs' visuals are powered by a proprietary liquid crystal on silicon (LCoS) display system, and even when used in a light-filled conference room, I could still clearly see the UI and its various apps. I tested out YouTube under these borderline abusive conditions, and it streamed high-def video in 16 million colors suitably.  The display offers a 51-degree field of view. It feels like having a large floating window hovering in front of you. From there, you can use simple gestures to launch apps, watch movies, play games, and do most other tasks you can’t do from your phone. But it was the context-aware, real-world spatial computing tasks that I wanted to try—the things you can't do from a phone or PC. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What can you actually do with a pair of Snap Specs? Snap plans to launch Specs with a full suite of both first-party and third-party apps that will do everything from improving your drawing skills to teaching you music. I tried out a golfing demo, and it made the possibilities of augmented reality glasses immediately clear. Instead of putting blindly toward a distant hole, Specs show you exactly which direction to swing the putter and adds a virtual flag to mark where the hole is. It’s anecdotal evidence, but my personal putting game improved immensely. Is it cheating? Probably, but it works. Are Specs going to be useful in the real world?A half-hour or so of testing a prototype isn’t enough time to really say whether these will be useful in a person’s real life, but I can say for sure that they’re very cool, and I’m looking forward to going more in-depth with them in the coming months as their release date approaches. Snap Specs are planned for release this fall and will retail for $2,195. (Thanks to Qualcomm for the trip to check out these glasses at Snapdragon Summit 2026)
